verdict.reasoning: Headache duration: “Had it for about a day now.” Location: “Mainly on the left side.” Quality and intermittency: “just kind of feels like it's throbbing… it kind of gets more or less severe,” and “When you say it comes and goes… it kind of gets more or less severe.”

Variable intensity: “it kind of gets more or less severe.” Worsened by light: “Kind of seems to be worse when I'm in a light room or like sunlight.” Improved by lying down: “I think I've generally been lying down. Seems to be better that way.”

No nausea/vomiting: “Any. Any nausea, vomiting? Patient: No, no, I've been feeling fine, actually.” No visual changes: “Any problems with your eyes or your eyesight? Patient: No, not at all.” No sensory symptoms: “any problems with weakness, tingling, numbness in your arms or legs? Patient: No, not at all.” No fever/cold: “feeling feverish, temperature, any runny nose, sore ears? Patient: No, not really… I was doing okay the day before.”
“Normally, do you get any headaches? Patient: No, not really. It's not something I've ever had before.” and “this headache is new to you and you've not had regular headaches before? Patient: Yeah.”
No menstrual association: “has it occurred at a particular time in your menstrual cycle? Patient: No, not particularly.” Last period ~1 week ago: “My period was about a week ago.”
Work stress as possible trigger: “Has anything changed recently or… might have triggered it? Patient: Not I can think of maybe a bit stressed out of work, that kind of thing.”
Past medical history: “In the past, have you had any significant medical problems? Any hospital admissions, operations, anything like that? Patient: No, not recently. Nothing.”

Contraception and duration: “Which contraception do you take? Patient: Microgynon.” and “When did you start that one? Patient: About six years ago.” Side effects: “Do you get any side effects from it? Patient: Not really, no. Not too much.”
Use of paracetamol: “What tablets have you been taking already for it? … Patient: Just paracetamol.”
NSAID use: “have you ever taken any non steroidal anti inflammatories like ibuprofen, naproxen, anything like that? Patient: I have in the past. I haven't been taking it last few days.”
Aspirin allergy and reaction: “I'm allergic to aspirin, so I haven't been taking that.” and “What happens when you take aspirin? Patient: I just feel really sick.”
Maternal hypertension: “anyone in your family had any medical problems? Patient: My mum had high blood pressure…”
Maternal migraine: “My mum had high blood pressure and she's got a history of migraines.”
Living situation: “Who do you live with at home? Patient: Just with housemates, just friends.”
Alcohol: “Do you drink much alcohol day today? Patient: I'd say a normal amount probably, you know, a few drinks at the weekend.”
Smoking: “Do you smoke? Patient: No.”
Drug use: “Do you take any other drugs of any sort? Patient: No.”
No vitals are mentioned anywhere in the transcript; no blood pressure, pulse, temperature, or other vital signs were documented.
The transcript does not describe the patient’s mental status, alertness, or orientation; no explicit or implicit statement like “alert and oriented” is present.

Neurological symptoms: “any problems with weakness, tingling, numbness in your arms or legs? Patient: No, not at all.” In this remote consultation, absence of reported focal deficits supports that no neurological deficits were found.

Acute new left-sided throbbing headache: supported by earlier HPI facts. Possible migraine: “it does sound quite like a migraine, but obviously you've had no history of that in the past.” New onset: “this headache is new to you and you've not had regular headaches before? Patient: Yeah.” Photophobia: “worse when I'm in a light room or like sunlight.”

Aspirin allergy limiting options is consistent with: “I'm allergic to aspirin… What happens when you take aspirin? Patient: I just feel really sick.” This allergy means some analgesic choices (e.g., aspirin) are restricted.

No systemic infection: no fever or infectious symptoms (“feeling feverish, temperature, any runny nose, sore ears? Patient: No, not really.”) and patient feels fine. No neurological emergency: no weakness, tingling, numbness, visual changes, or red‑flag symptoms are reported; the doctor manages conservatively and only advises to seek help if such symptoms develop.
Analgesia plan: “What I would suggest is taking some anti inflammatories along with a paracetamol.” This implies NSAIDs plus paracetamol, with prior discussion of allergy and tolerance.

Hydration advice is present: “Make sure you're really well hydrated and see how that goes.” However, there is no advice to rest or to avoid bright light; the doctor notes light worsens the headache but does not instruct “avoid bright light exposure.” Thus including rest and light avoidance overstates what was said.

Safety‑net advice: “if it isn't settling or it's getting worse or you get any other change in your headache or you're unwell with it with a high temperature, then we would certainly need to speak to you straight away…” and later “If you have a raised temperature or headaches just getting worse and we develop any rashes or anything like that, then we'd need to speak to you straight away.” Neurological symptom change is covered by “any other change in your headache” in this context.

BP and thermometer: “I would try and manage to get your blood pressure checked if you haven't had a chat for a while. Another thing to do is to have a thermometer at home so you make sure that your temperature is okay.”

Future follow‑up for persistent or cyclical headaches: “if you're getting persistent headaches or headaches associated with your menstrual cycle or certain things seem to trigger these headaches, then it would be worth having a further discussion about it to see whether we can work out if we can help that longer term.”
